english: worry; concern; something on your mind
usage: I have something on my mind
고민 + 이 있어요 = there is a worry
I have a lot on my mind
많다 = to be many; common with 고민
to worry; to think hard about
friendly way to ask what's wrong
examples: I have a lot on my mind these days.
I tell my worries to my friend.
nuance: 고민 is a worry or problem you keep thinking over, often a personal decision. It is softer and more everyday than 걱정, which is more about anxiety over a result. You can say 고민이 있어요 to mean you have something troubling you.
mistakes: Don't confuse 고민 (something you ponder) with 걱정 (anxious worry about an outcome).
To make the verb, add 하다: 고민하다, not 고민다.

usage: use 에 관심이 있어요 for the topic
examples: I'm not interested in that movie.
I'm really into exercise these days.
nuance: 관심 means interest or attention toward something or someone. The thing you are interested in takes the particle 에: 음악에 관심이 있어요. It can also mean caring attention, as in 관심을 가져 주세요 (please pay attention / care).
mistakes: Mark the topic with 에, not 를: 음악에 관심이 있어요, not 음악을 관심이 있어요.
Don't use 좋아하다 wording; say 관심이 있어요 to express having interest.

usage: 인내 + 심 is the common everyday form
examples: I'm a little short on patience.
nuance: 인내 is the abstract idea of patience or endurance, often in serious or formal contexts like study, work, or hardship. In everyday speech Koreans more often say 인내심 (patience as a trait) or 참다 (to put up with something). 인내 sounds a bit weighty and admirable.
mistakes: In casual talk, 인내심 sounds more natural than bare 인내.
Add 하다 for the verb: 인내하다, and remember 참다 covers everyday 'put up with'.

usage: 자신 + 감 is also very common
examples: I'm not confident about the test.
Now I've gained confidence in Korean.
nuance: 자신 here means confidence in your own ability, usually in 자신이 있어요/없어요. The same word 자신 can also mean 'oneself' (자기 자신 = one's own self). The closely related 자신감 names confidence as a feeling, while 자신이 있다 focuses on being sure you can do something.
mistakes: Mark the skill area with 에: 운동에 자신이 있어요.
Don't mix up 자신 (confidence/oneself) with 자신감; both exist, 자신감 is the feeling noun.

usage: 행복 + 하다 is the adjective form
examples: I'm happy being with my family.
I feel happiness in small things.
nuance: 행복 is happiness as a deep, lasting feeling of well-being, stronger than the everyday 기분이 좋다 (to be in a good mood). The adjective 행복하다 is used constantly: 행복해요. As a noun it appears in warm wishes like 행복하세요 (be happy) and 행복한 하루.
mistakes: 행복 is a noun; to say 'I'm happy' use the adjective 행복해요, not 행복이에요.
Don't confuse 행복 (deep happiness) with 기쁨 (joy from a specific event).

examples: Before a test I feel uneasy.
I feel a bit anxious when I'm alone.
I felt anxious after hearing the news.
nuance: 불안 is anxiety or an unsettled, restless feeling, the opposite of feeling secure (안심). The adjective 불안하다 is most common in speech: 불안해요. Use 마음이 불안하다 to say your heart feels uneasy. It is heavier than just 걱정 (worry).
mistakes: To say 'I'm anxious' use the adjective 불안해요, not 불안이에요.
불안 (unsettled feeling) differs from 걱정 (worrying about a specific thing).

examples: I'm really looking forward to tomorrow's trip.
I'm looking forward to the new movie.
If expectations are too big, you get disappointed.
nuance: 기대 is the happy feeling of looking forward to something, or an expectation you place on someone. The 되다 form 기대돼요 means 'I'm excited / I can't wait,' while 기대하다 means to expect or anticipate. With 기대돼요 the thing takes 이/가, not 을/를.
mistakes: With 기대되다 use 이/가: 여행이 기대돼요, not 여행을 기대돼요.
기대돼요 (it excites me) and 기대해요 (I expect/look forward) feel slightly different; learn both.

examples: I have a lot of free time on weekends.
nuance: 자유 means freedom or liberty, both the big idea and everyday 'doing as you please.' The adjective 자유롭다 (free, unrestricted) is common: 자유로워요. 자유 시간 is a very useful phrase for free time. It contrasts with feeling tied down or busy.
mistakes: The adjective is 자유롭다 → 자유로워요, not 자유하다.
Don't drop the space in 자유 시간 when writing it as two words.

english: greed; desire to have more; ambition
usage: to feel a desire (to have it)
examples: Seeing that bag, I really want it.
nuance: 욕심 is the wish to have or get more than you need, ranging from harmless wanting to real greed. 욕심이 나다 means something makes you want it, while 욕심이 많다 describes a greedy person. It can also be mild ambition, as in 욕심내서 공부해요 (study with drive).
mistakes: Use 나다 for the urge: 욕심이 나요, not 욕심을 해요.
욕심 (wanting more) is not the neutral 원하다 (to want); it carries a 'too much' nuance.

usage: to put one's whole heart in
examples: Mom prepares the meal with all her heart.
This gift is full of heartfelt care.
I wrote the letter with all my heart.
nuance: 정성 is the warm, careful effort you put into something for someone, like cooking, a gift, or a letter. The adverb 정성껏 (wholeheartedly) is very useful. It shows that care and sincerity, not just the result, matter, and Koreans value it highly in everyday kindness.
mistakes: 정성껏 is an adverb; don't add 하게 to it.
정성 (heartfelt effort) is broader than mere 노력 (effort); it stresses warmth and care.

examples: My friend's words were a big comfort.
When it's hard, I need comfort.
따뜻한 차 한 잔이 위로가 돼요.
A warm cup of tea is comforting.
nuance: 위로 is comfort or consolation given to someone who is sad or struggling. 위로가 되다 means something brings comfort, and 위로하다 means to comfort another person. It is a gentle, caring word used often when friends support each other through hard times.
mistakes: Use 되다 for 'is comforting': 위로가 돼요, not 위로해요 (which means 'I comfort someone').
To comfort a person, mark them with 를: 친구를 위로해요.

usage: to become a source of pride
examples: My friend is showing off a new car.
The son is his parents' pride.
nuance: 자랑 covers both honest pride and boastful showing off, depending on context. 자랑하다 often means to brag, which can sound a little negative, while the adjective 자랑스럽다 (proud) is purely positive. Saying 우리 가족 자랑 means 'the pride of our family.'
mistakes: 자랑하다 (to brag) can sound boastful; for 'I'm proud' use 자랑스럽다.
Mark what you show off with 를: 사진을 자랑해요.

nuance: 평화 means peace, both in the big sense of no conflict and the everyday feeling of calm. The adjective 평화롭다 (peaceful) is common for quiet, relaxing scenes: 평화로워요. The phrase 마음의 평화 (peace of mind) is a nice way to talk about inner calm.
mistakes: The adjective is 평화롭다 → 평화로워요, not 평화하다.
Don't confuse 평화 (peace/calm) with 평소 (usual times).
